en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 147, the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta (The Shorter Discourse of Advice to Rāhula).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“The qualities that ripen for liberation have indeed matured in Rāhula.”
"What if I were to further train Rāhula for the destruction of the taints?
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the almsround after his meal, he addressed the Venerable Rāhula:
“Take your sitting cloth, Rāhula;
we will go to the Blind Men’s Grove for the day’s abiding.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Rāhula replied to the Blessed One, and taking his sitting cloth, he followed closely behind the Blessed One.
Now at that time, many thousands of deities followed after the Blessed One, thinking:
"Today the Blessed One will further train the Venerable Rāhula for the destruction of the taints.
Then the Blessed One, having entered deep into the Andhavana grove, sat down on a seat prepared at the foot of a certain tree.
The Venerable Rāhula also paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Rāhula was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“What do you think, Rāhula?”
“Is the eye permanent or impermanent?”—
“Impermanent, venerable sir.”—
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, Bhante.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“What do you think, Rāhula,
are forms permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Rāhula,
is eye-consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”—
“Suffering, Bhante.”—
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante.”—
“What do you think, Rāhula?”
“Is eye-contact permanent or impermanent?”—
“Impermanent, venerable sir.”—
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“What do you think, Rāhula,
is that which arises conditioned by eye-contact— whether it belongs to feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness— permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“What do you think, Rāhula, is the ear permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.
“… Is the nose permanent or impermanent?”

“Is the body permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.
“Is the mind permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, Bhante.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, Bhante.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Rāhula, are mental phenomena permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, Bhante.
“What do you think, Rāhula, is mind-consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“What do you think, Rāhula, is mind-contact permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Rāhula,
is that which arises conditioned by mind-contact— whether it belongs to feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness— permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, Bhante.
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante.”—
“Seeing thus, Rāhula, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms...”

One becomes disenchanted with eye-consciousness; one becomes disenchanted with eye-contact; and one becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness arise conditioned by that eye-contact.
One becomes disenchanted with the ear; one becomes disenchanted with sounds … [and so forth].
One becomes disenchanted with the nose, one becomes disenchanted with odors...
one becomes disenchanted with the tongue, one becomes disenchanted with tastes...
one becomes disenchanted with the body, one becomes disenchanted with tangibles...
One becomes disenchanted with the mind, one becomes disenchanted with mental phenomena, one becomes disenchanted with mind-consciousness, one becomes disenchanted with mind-contact;
and one also becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness arise conditioned by mind-contact.
“Becoming disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. One understands:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Rāhula was uplifted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
While this exposition was being spoken, the Venerable Rāhula’s mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
And in those many thousands of deities, the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose: [that whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation].
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.
The Shorter Discourse of Advice to Rāhula is finished; it is the fifth.
